summary.zh: 本课程深入探讨了分词在语言建模中的核心作用，从基础概念到BPE和Unigram算法的机制与实现。首先，解释了为什么分词是模型处理文本的关键步骤，涉及分词、子词和词表的定义。其次，详细分析了BPE和Unigram的原理，包括数学公式和工程参数选择。最后，通过多语种分词的实践示例，展示了如何构建可复现流程并计算评估指标。课程强调理论结合实践，帮助学习者掌握从传统NLP到LLM的关键概念链条，并应用于提示工程等场景。
summary.en: This course delves into the core role of tokenization in language modeling, from fundamental concepts to the mechanisms and implementation of BPE and Unigram algorithms. First, it explains why tokenization is a critical step for models to process text, covering definitions of tokenization, subwords, and vocabulary. Second, it provides a detailed analysis of BPE and Unigram principles, including mathematical formulas and engineering parameter selection. Finally, through a practical example of multilingual tokenization, it demonstrates how to build a reproducible pipeline and compute evaluation metrics. The course emphasizes combining theory with practice, helping learners master key conceptual chains from traditional NLP to LLMs and apply them in scenarios like prompt engineering.

content.zh:
从字符到Token：为什么需要分词？

在自然语言处理（Natural Language Processing, NLP）中，语言模型（Language Model, LM）无法直接处理原始文本字符串。文本由字符序列组成，而字符本身缺乏语义信息。例如，英文单词“unhappiness”包含13个字符，但模型需要理解其作为“un-”（否定前缀）、“happi”（词根）和“-ness”（名词后缀）的组合。分词（Tokenization）正是将连续文本转换为离散单元（tokens）的过程，这些单元可以是单词、子词（subword）或字符，构成模型输入的基础。在大型语言模型（Large Language Model, LLM）如GPT系列中，分词决定了模型如何“看到”文本，直接影响其理解和生成能力。这一步骤是语言建模的基石，尤其在提示工程（Prompt Engineering）中，token数量直接关联上下文窗口限制。

精确定义上，分词指将文本分割为tokens的算法或流程。关键术语包括：分词（Tokenization）、子词（Subword，介于字符和完整词之间的文本单元）、词表（Vocabulary，所有可能tokens的集合）。例如，在中文中，“自然语言处理”可能被分词为[“自然”, “语言”, “处理”]，而在子词分词中，英文“lower”可能被分解为[“low”, “er”]。分词的目标是平衡词表大小和语义粒度：词表过大会导致稀疏性问题，过小则丢失语义细节。数学上，分词可视为一个映射函数 \( f: T \rightarrow V \)，其中 \( T \) 是文本空间，\( V \) 是词表索引空间，目标是最大化文本的压缩效率或语言模型概率。

机制上，分词的核心是选择合适的分割策略。传统方法如空格分割（whitespace tokenization）简单但局限，无法处理无空格语言（如中文）或复合词（如“New York”）。更先进的方法基于统计或神经网络，例如BPE（Byte Pair Encoding，字节对编码）和Unigram（一元语言模型）。评估分词质量常用指标包括压缩率（Compression Ratio），定义为原始文本长度与token数量的比值：\( CR = \frac{L_{\text{text}}}{N_{\text{tokens}}} \)，其中 \( L_{\text{text}} \) 是字符数，\( N_{\text{tokens}} \) 是token数。高压缩率表示更高效的表示，但可能牺牲语义。另一个关键指标是词汇覆盖率（Vocabulary Coverage），衡量词表覆盖训练数据中不同文本单元的比例。

工程实现中，分词流程包括文本预处理（如规范化、去除特殊字符）、分词算法应用和词表构建。关键要点是处理多语言文本时需统一编码（如UTF-8），并考虑语言特异性。例如，英文可能使用BPE，而中文可能基于字符或词分割。复杂度方面，分词通常是 \( O(n) \) 线性时间，但词表大小影响内存使用。延迟敏感点包括分词器的初始化和批量处理优化。在提示工程中，分词影响提示长度计算，例如GPT-3的上下文窗口以tokens计，而非字符，这要求工程师精确控制输入规模。

常见误区包括认为分词仅是空格分割，或一个词表可处理所有语言。失败模式可能源于未处理罕见字符或编码错误，导致模型输入噪声。诊断方法包括检查token分布（如频率直方图）和对比不同分词器的输出。例如，如果token数量异常高，可能指示过度分割。另一个误区是忽视分词对模型性能的间接影响，如过大的词表增加训练成本。通过可视化token序列和计算指标如词汇覆盖率，可评估分词效果。实践中，建议使用标准化工具如SentencePiece（来源：SentencePiece: A simple and language independent subword tokenizer and detokenizer for Neural Text Processing, 2018）来避免常见陷阱。

理解了分词的基础作用和挑战，我们接下来深入两种主流算法：BPE和Unigram，它们如何从不同角度优化分词过程，并为多语种处理奠定基础。

BPE与Unigram：两种子词算法的核心思想

BPE（Byte Pair Encoding，字节对编码）和Unigram（Unigram Language Model，一元语言模型）是子词分词（Subword Tokenization）的两种核心算法，广泛应用于现代语言模型如BERT和GPT。BPE起源于数据压缩领域，通过迭代合并频繁字符对构建词表；Unigram则基于概率模型，选择最大化整体概率的分词方案。两者都旨在解决词汇表外（Out-of-Vocabulary, OOV）词问题，但机制不同：BPE是贪婪的、确定性的，而Unigram是概率性的、可提供多个候选。在语言建模中，这些算法帮助模型处理未见词汇，提升泛化能力。

精确定义上，BPE是一种基于频率的合并算法，核心思想是逐步将最常见字符对（character pair）合并为新token，直到达到预设词表大小。Unigram是一种语言模型分词方法，假设每个token独立，通过最大化序列概率 \( P(\mathbf{x}) = \prod_{i} P(t_i) \) 来选择分词，其中 \( t_i \) 是token，\( P(t_i) \) 从其频率估计。关键术语包括：字节对编码（Byte Pair Encoding, BPE）、一元语言模型（Unigram Language Model）、合并操作（Merge Operation）。例如，在BPE中，如果“e”和“s”频繁共现，它们可能合并为“es”。这些定义源自经典论文（来源：Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units, 2015）。

机制上，BPE算法步骤包括：初始化词表为所有字符；计算所有相邻字符对频率；合并最高频对；重复直到词表大小达标。数学上，合并准则基于频率最大化：\( \text{merge} = \arg\max_{(a,b)} \text{freq}(a,b) \)，其中 \( a \) 和 \( b \) 是字符或现有tokens。Unigram则通过动态规划求解最优分词，目标函数是 \( \max_{\mathbf{t}} \sum_{i} \log P(t_i) \)，其中 \( P(t_i) \) 通常用最大似然估计（Maximum Likelihood Estimation, MLE）从训练数据学习。Unigram还可通过退火（Annealing）调整概率，生成多样分词，如论文所述（来源：Subword Regularization: Improving Neural Network Translation Models with Multiple Subword Candidates, 2018）。

工程实现要点包括：BPE需维护频率表，复杂度为 \( O(k \cdot n) \)，其中 \( k \) 是合并次数，\( n \) 是文本长度；Unigram需预计算token概率，可能使用维特比算法（Viterbi Algorithm）进行高效解码。参数选择上，BPE的词表大小是关键，通常基于验证集性能调整；Unigram则需设置平滑参数避免零概率。在工具层面，SentencePiece库实现了两者，支持多语言。例如，训练BPE分词器时，过小的词表可能导致信息丢失，而过大会增加过拟合风险。实际中，建议从较小词表开始，逐步扩展。

常见误区包括认为BPE总是优于Unigram，或忽视算法对语言特性的适应性。失败模式可能源于训练数据偏差，如BPE在低资源语言上合并无意义对。诊断方法包括分析合并历史和比较不同参数下的分词质量。例如，如果BPE产生过多罕见tokens，可能需要调整词表大小或预处理。另一个误区是混淆BPE与WordPiece（后者类似但合并准则不同）。通过计算指标如分词一致性（Tokenization Consistency），可评估算法稳定性。实践中，混合使用BPE和Unigram可能在某些场景更优。

掌握了BPE和Unigram的原理，我们转向多语种场景，探讨如何在实际工程中应用这些算法处理复杂文本，并构建可复现的流程。

多语种分词的工程实践

多语种分词（Multilingual Tokenization）涉及处理混合语言文本，如中英文混合“Hello 世界”，需考虑语言特异性、字符编码和模型兼容性。随着全球化应用增多，如机器翻译或跨语言检索，高效的多语言分词成为关键。挑战包括语言识别（Language Identification）、处理不同书写系统（如拉丁字母vs.汉字）和平衡词表大小。例如，中文通常按字符分词，而英文可能用BPE，混合时需协调策略。这要求工程师理解Unicode编码和语言检测技术。

精确定义上，多语种分词指为多种语言设计统一或混合的分词流程。关键术语包括：Unicode（统一字符编码标准）、语言标识（Language Identification）、特殊token（Special Tokens，如[CLS]、[SEP]）。例如，在Transformer模型中，特殊token用于分隔序列或表示任务。数学上，多语言分词可视为一个优化问题：最小化整体困惑度（Perplexity）或最大化跨语言对齐（Cross-lingual Alignment）。评估指标常用双语评估替分（BLEU, Bilingual Evaluation Understudy），但针对分词，可使用token重叠率（Token Overlap Rate）：\( \text{TOR} = \frac{|\text{tokens}_1 \cap \text{tokens}_2|}{\max(|\text{tokens}_1|, |\text{tokens}_2|)} \)，比较不同分词器的输出一致性。

机制上，多语种分词流程包括：文本预处理（统一为UTF-8编码）、语言检测（可用库如langdetect）、应用语言特定分词器、后处理（如添加特殊token）。工程实现要点是使用灵活的工具如SentencePiece，它支持从混合语料训练单一分词器，通过Unicode编码处理多语言。例如，SentencePiece将文本视为Unicode字符序列，无需预先分词，从而支持无空格语言。复杂度方面，语言检测增加 \( O(n) \) 开销，但可缓存结果优化。根据官方文档（来源：SentencePiece GitHub Repository），该工具简化了多语言处理。

在实现中，关键步骤是训练分词器：收集多语言数据、清洗（去除噪声）、训练BPE或Unigram模型。例如，为处理中英文，可混合使用中文维基百科和英文新闻数据。失败模式可能源于编码错误（如非UTF-8字符）或语言误判，导致分词错误。诊断方法包括检查token分布按语言和可视化分词边界。另一个常见误区是假设一个词表适用于所有语言；实际上，不同语言可能需要不同粒度，如中文字符vs.英文子词。通过以下综合示例，我们构建一个可复现的多语言分词流程，应用BPE和Unigram，并计算评估指标以巩固理解。

import sentencepiece as spm
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

# Step 1: Construct mixed Chinese-English text data (inline, no external files)
texts = [
    "Hello world",
    "你好世界",
    "Hello 世界",
    "Natural Language Processing 自然语言处理",
    "Tokenization is a fundamental step"
]
print("Original text examples:")
for t in texts[:3]:
    print(f"  {t}")
print(f"Data scale: {len(texts)} texts")

# Step 2: Text cleaning (simple removal of extra spaces, may need more in practice)
cleaned_texts = [t.strip() for t in texts]

# Step 3: Train BPE tokenizer (using inline data, avoiding temporary files)
corpus_text = '\n'.join(cleaned_texts)
spm.SentencePieceTrainer.train(
    sentence_iterator=iter([corpus_text]),
    model_prefix='bpe_model',
    vocab_size=50,  # Small vocabulary for demonstration
    model_type='bpe',
    input_format='text'
)
sp_bpe = spm.SentencePieceProcessor(model_file='bpe_model.model')

# Train Unigram tokenizer
spm.SentencePieceTrainer.train(
    sentence_iterator=iter([corpus_text]),
    model_prefix='unigram_model',
    vocab_size=50,
    model_type='unigram',
    input_format='text'
)
sp_uni = spm.SentencePieceProcessor(model_file='unigram_model.model')

print(f"BPE vocabulary size: {sp_bpe.get_piece_size()}")
print(f"Unigram vocabulary size: {sp_uni.get_piece_size()}")

# Step 4: Apply tokenizers to new text
sample_text = "Hello 世界 Tokenization"
tokens_bpe = sp_bpe.encode_as_pieces(sample_text)
tokens_uni = sp_uni.encode_as_pieces(sample_text)
print(f"Sample text: {sample_text}")
print(f"BPE tokenization result: {tokens_bpe}")
print(f"Unigram tokenization result: {tokens_uni}")

# Step 5: Compute evaluation metric - Token Overlap Rate (TOR)
def token_overlap_rate(tokens1, tokens2):
    set1, set2 = set(tokens1), set(tokens2)
    overlap = len(set1.intersection(set2))
    max_len = max(len(set1), len(set2))
    return overlap / max_len if max_len > 0 else 0.0

tor = token_overlap_rate(tokens_bpe, tokens_uni)
print(f"Token Overlap Rate (TOR) between BPE and Unigram: {tor:.3f}")
print("Formula: TOR = |tokens1 ∩ tokens2| / max(|tokens1|, |tokens2|)")

# Print intermediate variables
print(f"BPE token sequence length: {len(tokens_bpe)}")
print(f"Unigram token sequence length: {len(tokens_uni)}")

# Clean up temporary files
import os
if os.path.exists('bpe_model.model'):
    os.remove('bpe_model.model')
if os.path.exists('bpe_model.vocab'):
    os.remove('bpe_model.vocab')
if os.path.exists('unigram_model.model'):
    os.remove('unigram_model.model')
if os.path.exists('unigram_model.vocab'):
    os.remove('unigram_model.vocab')

此示例展示了端到端流程：从内联数据构造、清洗、训练BPE和Unigram分词器，到应用和评估。输出包括原始文本、词表大小、分词结果和TOR指标。TOR计算了两种算法分词结果的重叠程度，值越高表示一致性越好；这里TOR较低，反映BPE和Unigram在不同语言上的策略差异。通过调整vocab_size或添加更多数据，可优化分词效果。此代码完全可复现，无需外部文件，依赖仅sentencepiece。轻量替代方案：若无法安装sentencepiece，可用简单规则分词（如按空格和字符分割）作为baseline，但会损失子词优势。

总结来说，分词是语言模型的基石，BPE和Unigram提供了灵活的子词解决方案，而多语种处理需结合语言特性和工程实践。掌握这些概念，您能更有效地设计提示和理解模型行为，为高级NLP任务打下基础。
content.en:
From Characters to Tokens: Why Tokenization Matters

In natural language processing (NLP), language models (LMs) cannot directly process raw text strings. Text consists of character sequences, but characters themselves lack semantic information. For example, the English word "unhappiness" contains 13 characters, but a model needs to understand it as a combination of "un-" (negation prefix), "happi" (stem), and "-ness" (noun suffix). Tokenization is the process of converting continuous text into discrete units called tokens, which can be words, subwords, or characters, forming the foundation of model input. In large language models (LLMs) like the GPT series, tokenization determines how the model "sees" text, directly impacting its comprehension and generation capabilities. This step is fundamental to language modeling, especially in prompt engineering, where token count relates directly to context window limits.

Precisely defined, tokenization refers to the algorithm or pipeline that segments text into tokens. Key terms include: Tokenization, Subword (text units between characters and full words), and Vocabulary (the set of all possible tokens). For instance, in Chinese, "自然语言处理" might be tokenized into ["自然", "语言", "处理"], while in subword tokenization, English "lower" might be decomposed into ["low", "er"]. The goal of tokenization is to balance vocabulary size and semantic granularity: an overly large vocabulary leads to sparsity issues, while an overly small one loses semantic detail. Mathematically, tokenization can be viewed as a mapping function \( f: T \rightarrow V \), where \( T \) is the text space and \( V \) is the vocabulary index space, aiming to maximize compression efficiency or language model probability.

Mechanistically, the core of tokenization is selecting an appropriate segmentation strategy. Traditional methods like whitespace tokenization are simple but limited, unable to handle languages without spaces (e.g., Chinese) or compound words (e.g., "New York"). More advanced methods are based on statistics or neural networks, such as BPE (Byte Pair Encoding) and Unigram (Unigram Language Model). Common metrics for evaluating tokenization quality include compression ratio, defined as the ratio of original text length to token count: \( CR = \frac{L_{\text{text}}}{N_{\text{tokens}}} \), where \( L_{\text{text}} \) is the character count and \( N_{\text{tokens}} \) is the token count. A high compression ratio indicates more efficient representation but may sacrifice semantics. Another key metric is vocabulary coverage, measuring the proportion of different text units in training data covered by the vocabulary.

In engineering implementation, the tokenization pipeline includes text preprocessing (e.g., normalization, removing special characters), applying tokenization algorithms, and vocabulary construction. A key point is that handling multilingual text requires unified encoding (e.g., UTF-8) and consideration of language specificity. For example, English might use BPE, while Chinese might be segmented by characters or words. In terms of complexity, tokenization is typically \( O(n) \) linear time, but vocabulary size affects memory usage. Latency-sensitive aspects include tokenizer initialization and batch processing optimization. In prompt engineering, tokenization influences prompt length calculation, e.g., GPT-3's context window is measured in tokens, not characters, requiring engineers to precisely control input scale.

Common misconceptions include thinking tokenization is merely splitting by spaces, or that one vocabulary can handle all languages. Failure modes may arise from not handling rare characters or encoding errors, leading to noisy model input. Diagnostic methods include checking token distributions (e.g., frequency histograms) and comparing outputs from different tokenizers. For instance, if the token count is abnormally high, it may indicate over-segmentation. Another misconception is neglecting the indirect impact of tokenization on model performance, such as increased training costs with large vocabularies. By visualizing token sequences and computing metrics like vocabulary coverage, one can assess tokenization effectiveness. In practice, using standardized tools like SentencePiece (source: SentencePiece: A simple and language independent subword tokenizer and detokenizer for Neural Text Processing, 2018) helps avoid common pitfalls.

Understanding the foundational role and challenges of tokenization, we now delve into two mainstream algorithms: BPE and Unigram, which optimize the tokenization process from different angles and lay the groundwork for multilingual handling.

BPE and Unigram: Core Ideas of Two Subword Algorithms

BPE (Byte Pair Encoding) and Unigram (Unigram Language Model) are two core algorithms for subword tokenization, widely used in modern language models like BERT and GPT. BPE originates from data compression, building vocabularies by iteratively merging frequent character pairs; Unigram is based on a probabilistic model, selecting segmentation that maximizes overall probability. Both aim to address out-of-vocabulary (OOV) word issues, but their mechanisms differ: BPE is greedy and deterministic, while Unigram is probabilistic and can provide multiple candidates. In language modeling, these algorithms help models handle unseen vocabulary, improving generalization.

Precisely defined, BPE is a frequency-based merging algorithm whose core idea is to gradually merge the most common character pairs into new tokens until a preset vocabulary size is reached. Unigram is a language model tokenization method that assumes each token is independent, selecting segmentation by maximizing sequence probability \( P(\mathbf{x}) = \prod_{i} P(t_i) \), where \( t_i \) is a token and \( P(t_i) \) is estimated from its frequency. Key terms include: Byte Pair Encoding (BPE), Unigram Language Model, and Merge Operation. For example, in BPE, if "e" and "s" co-occur frequently, they might merge into "es". These definitions stem from classic papers (source: Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units, 2015).

Mechanistically, the BPE algorithm steps include: initializing the vocabulary with all characters; computing frequencies of all adjacent character pairs; merging the highest-frequency pair; repeating until vocabulary size is met. Mathematically, the merging criterion is based on frequency maximization: \( \text{merge} = \arg\max_{(a,b)} \text{freq}(a,b) \), where \( a \) and \( b \) are characters or existing tokens. Unigram solves for optimal segmentation via dynamic programming, with the objective function \( \max_{\mathbf{t}} \sum_{i} \log P(t_i) \), where \( P(t_i) \) is typically learned from training data using maximum likelihood estimation (MLE). Unigram can also adjust probabilities through annealing to generate diverse segmentations, as described in papers (source: Subword Regularization: Improving Neural Network Translation Models with Multiple Subword Candidates, 2018).

Engineering implementation points include: BPE requires maintaining a frequency table, with complexity \( O(k \cdot n) \), where \( k \) is the number of merges and \( n \) is text length; Unigram needs precomputed token probabilities, possibly using the Viterbi algorithm for efficient decoding. In parameter selection, BPE's vocabulary size is critical, usually tuned based on validation set performance; Unigram requires smoothing parameters to avoid zero probabilities. At the tool level, the SentencePiece library implements both, supporting multiple languages. For example, when training a BPE tokenizer, too small a vocabulary may lose information, while too large increases overfitting risk. In practice, starting with a smaller vocabulary and gradually expanding is recommended.

Common misconceptions include thinking BPE is always better than Unigram, or ignoring algorithm adaptability to language characteristics. Failure modes may stem from training data bias, e.g., BPE merging meaningless pairs in low-resource languages. Diagnostic methods include analyzing merge histories and comparing segmentation quality under different parameters. For instance, if BPE produces too many rare tokens, adjusting vocabulary size or preprocessing may be needed. Another misconception is confusing BPE with WordPiece (the latter is similar but has a different merging criterion). By computing metrics like tokenization consistency, one can evaluate algorithm stability. In practice, hybrid use of BPE and Unigram may be optimal in certain scenarios.

Having grasped the principles of BPE and Unigram, we turn to multilingual scenarios, exploring how to apply these algorithms in practical engineering to handle complex texts and build reproducible pipelines.

Engineering Practices for Multilingual Tokenization

Multilingual tokenization involves processing mixed-language texts, such as Chinese-English "Hello 世界", requiring consideration of language specificity, character encoding, and model compatibility. With the rise of global applications like machine translation or cross-lingual retrieval, efficient multilingual tokenization becomes crucial. Challenges include language identification, handling different writing systems (e.g., Latin alphabet vs. Chinese characters), and balancing vocabulary sizes. For example, Chinese is often tokenized by characters, while English might use BPE, necessitating coordinated strategies for mixtures. This requires engineers to understand Unicode encoding and language detection techniques.

Precisely defined, multilingual tokenization refers to designing unified or hybrid tokenization pipelines for multiple languages. Key terms include: Unicode (the universal character encoding standard), Language Identification, and Special Tokens (e.g., [CLS], [SEP]). For instance, in Transformer models, special tokens are used to separate sequences or represent tasks. Mathematically, multilingual tokenization can be viewed as an optimization problem: minimizing overall perplexity or maximizing cross-lingual alignment. Common evaluation metrics include BLEU (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy), but for tokenization, token overlap rate can be used: \( \text{TOR} = \frac{|\text{tokens}_1 \cap \text{tokens}_2|}{\max(|\text{tokens}_1|, |\text{tokens}_2|)} \), comparing output consistency across tokenizers.

Mechanistically, the multilingual tokenization pipeline includes: text preprocessing (unifying to UTF-8 encoding), language detection (using libraries like langdetect), applying language-specific tokenizers, and post-processing (e.g., adding special tokens). An engineering key point is using flexible tools like SentencePiece, which supports training a single tokenizer from mixed corpora, handling multiple languages via Unicode encoding. For example, SentencePiece treats text as Unicode character sequences, requiring no pre-tokenization, thus supporting languages without spaces. In terms of complexity, language detection adds \( O(n) \) overhead but can be optimized by caching results. According to official documentation (source: SentencePiece GitHub Repository), this tool simplifies multilingual processing.

In implementation, a key step is training the tokenizer: collecting multilingual data, cleaning (removing noise), and training BPE or Unigram models. For instance, to handle Chinese-English, one might mix Chinese Wikipedia and English news data. Failure modes may arise from encoding errors (e.g., non-UTF-8 characters) or language misidentification, leading to incorrect tokenization. Diagnostic methods include checking token distributions by language and visualizing segmentation boundaries. Another common misconception is assuming one vocabulary suits all languages; in reality, different languages may require different granularities, such as Chinese characters vs. English subwords. Through the following comprehensive example, we build a reproducible multilingual tokenization pipeline, applying BPE and Unigram, and compute evaluation metrics to solidify understanding.

import sentencepiece as spm
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

# Step 1: Construct mixed Chinese-English text data (inline, no external files)
texts = [
    "Hello world",
    "你好世界",
    "Hello 世界",
    "Natural Language Processing 自然语言处理",
    "Tokenization is a fundamental step"
]
print("Original text examples:")
for t in texts[:3]:
    print(f"  {t}")
print(f"Data scale: {len(texts)} texts")

# Step 2: Text cleaning (simple removal of extra spaces, may need more in practice)
cleaned_texts = [t.strip() for t in texts]

# Step 3: Train BPE tokenizer (using inline data, avoiding temporary files)
corpus_text = '\n'.join(cleaned_texts)
spm.SentencePieceTrainer.train(
    sentence_iterator=iter([corpus_text]),
    model_prefix='bpe_model',
    vocab_size=50,  # Small vocabulary for demonstration
    model_type='bpe',
    input_format='text'
)
sp_bpe = spm.SentencePieceProcessor(model_file='bpe_model.model')

# Train Unigram tokenizer
spm.SentencePieceTrainer.train(
    sentence_iterator=iter([corpus_text]),
    model_prefix='unigram_model',
    vocab_size=50,
    model_type='unigram',
    input_format='text'
)
sp_uni = spm.SentencePieceProcessor(model_file='unigram_model.model')

print(f"BPE vocabulary size: {sp_bpe.get_piece_size()}")
print(f"Unigram vocabulary size: {sp_uni.get_piece_size()}")

# Step 4: Apply tokenizers to new text
sample_text = "Hello 世界 Tokenization"
tokens_bpe = sp_bpe.encode_as_pieces(sample_text)
tokens_uni = sp_uni.encode_as_pieces(sample_text)
print(f"Sample text: {sample_text}")
print(f"BPE tokenization result: {tokens_bpe}")
print(f"Unigram tokenization result: {tokens_uni}")

# Step 5: Compute evaluation metric - Token Overlap Rate (TOR)
def token_overlap_rate(tokens1, tokens2):
    set1, set2 = set(tokens1), set(tokens2)
    overlap = len(set1.intersection(set2))
    max_len = max(len(set1), len(set2))
    return overlap / max_len if max_len > 0 else 0.0

tor = token_overlap_rate(tokens_bpe, tokens_uni)
print(f"Token Overlap Rate (TOR) between BPE and Unigram: {tor:.3f}")
print("Formula: TOR = |tokens1 ∩ tokens2| / max(|tokens1|, |tokens2|)")

# Print intermediate variables
print(f"BPE token sequence length: {len(tokens_bpe)}")
print(f"Unigram token sequence length: {len(tokens_uni)}")

# Clean up temporary files
import os
if os.path.exists('bpe_model.model'):
    os.remove('bpe_model.model')
if os.path.exists('bpe_model.vocab'):
    os.remove('bpe_model.vocab')
if os.path.exists('unigram_model.model'):
    os.remove('unigram_model.model')
if os.path.exists('unigram_model.vocab'):
    os.remove('unigram_model.vocab')

This example demonstrates an end-to-end pipeline: from inline data construction, cleaning, training BPE and Unigram tokenizers, to application and evaluation. Outputs include original texts, vocabulary sizes, tokenization results, and the TOR metric. TOR calculates the overlap between tokenization results from the two algorithms, with higher values indicating better consistency; here, a low TOR reflects strategic differences between BPE and Unigram across languages. By adjusting vocab_size or adding more data, tokenization can be optimized. This code is fully reproducible, requiring no external files and dependencies only on sentencepiece. Lightweight alternative: if sentencepiece cannot be installed, simple rule-based tokenization (e.g., splitting by spaces and characters) can serve as a baseline, but loses subword advantages.

In summary, tokenization is the cornerstone of language models, with BPE and Unigram offering flexible subword solutions, while multilingual handling requires combining language characteristics and engineering practices. Mastering these concepts enables more effective prompt design and model behavior understanding, laying a foundation for advanced NLP tasks.

summary.en: This course delves into the core role of tokenization in language modeling, from fundamental concepts to the mechanisms and implementation of BPE and Unigram algorithms. First, it explains why tokenization is a critical step for models to process text, covering definitions of tokenization, subwords, and vocabulary. Second, it provides a detailed analysis of BPE and Unigram principles, including mathematical formulas and engineering parameter selection. Finally, through a practical example of multilingual tokenization, it demonstrates how to build a reproducible pipeline and compute evaluation metrics. The course emphasizes combining theory with practice, helping learners master key conceptual chains from traditional NLP to LLMs and apply them in scenarios like prompt engineering.

content.zh:
从字符到Token：为什么需要分词？

在自然语言处理（Natural Language Processing, NLP）中，语言模型（Language Model, LM）无法直接处理原始文本字符串。文本由字符序列组成，而字符本身缺乏语义信息。例如，英文单词“unhappiness”包含13个字符，但模型需要理解其作为“un-”（否定前缀）、“happi”（词根）和“-ness”（名词后缀）的组合。分词（Tokenization）正是将连续文本转换为离散单元（tokens）的过程，这些单元可以是单词、子词（subword）或字符，构成模型输入的基础。在大型语言模型（Large Language Model, LLM）如GPT系列中，分词决定了模型如何“看到”文本，直接影响其理解和生成能力。这一步骤是语言建模的基石，尤其在提示工程（Prompt Engineering）中，token数量直接关联上下文窗口限制。

精确定义上，分词指将文本分割为tokens的算法或流程。关键术语包括：分词（Tokenization）、子词（Subword，介于字符和完整词之间的文本单元）、词表（Vocabulary，所有可能tokens的集合）。例如，在中文中，“自然语言处理”可能被分词为[“自然”, “语言”, “处理”]，而在子词分词中，英文“lower”可能被分解为[“low”, “er”]。分词的目标是平衡词表大小和语义粒度：词表过大会导致稀疏性问题，过小则丢失语义细节。数学上，分词可视为一个映射函数 \( f: T \rightarrow V \)，其中 \( T \) 是文本空间，\( V \) 是词表索引空间，目标是最大化文本的压缩效率或语言模型概率。

机制上，分词的核心是选择合适的分割策略。传统方法如空格分割（whitespace tokenization）简单但局限，无法处理无空格语言（如中文）或复合词（如“New York”）。更先进的方法基于统计或神经网络，例如BPE（Byte Pair Encoding，字节对编码）和Unigram（一元语言模型）。评估分词质量常用指标包括压缩率（Compression Ratio），定义为原始文本长度与token数量的比值：\( CR = \frac{L_{\text{text}}}{N_{\text{tokens}}} \)，其中 \( L_{\text{text}} \) 是字符数，\( N_{\text{tokens}} \) 是token数。高压缩率表示更高效的表示，但可能牺牲语义。另一个关键指标是词汇覆盖率（Vocabulary Coverage），衡量词表覆盖训练数据中不同文本单元的比例。

工程实现中，分词流程包括文本预处理（如规范化、去除特殊字符）、分词算法应用和词表构建。关键要点是处理多语言文本时需统一编码（如UTF-8），并考虑语言特异性。例如，英文可能使用BPE，而中文可能基于字符或词分割。复杂度方面，分词通常是 \( O(n) \) 线性时间，但词表大小影响内存使用。延迟敏感点包括分词器的初始化和批量处理优化。在提示工程中，分词影响提示长度计算，例如GPT-3的上下文窗口以tokens计，而非字符，这要求工程师精确控制输入规模。

常见误区包括认为分词仅是空格分割，或一个词表可处理所有语言。失败模式可能源于未处理罕见字符或编码错误，导致模型输入噪声。诊断方法包括检查token分布（如频率直方图）和对比不同分词器的输出。例如，如果token数量异常高，可能指示过度分割。另一个误区是忽视分词对模型性能的间接影响，如过大的词表增加训练成本。通过可视化token序列和计算指标如词汇覆盖率，可评估分词效果。实践中，建议使用标准化工具如SentencePiece（来源：SentencePiece: A simple and language independent subword tokenizer and detokenizer for Neural Text Processing, 2018）来避免常见陷阱。

理解了分词的基础作用和挑战，我们接下来深入两种主流算法：BPE和Unigram，它们如何从不同角度优化分词过程，并为多语种处理奠定基础。

BPE与Unigram：两种子词算法的核心思想

BPE（Byte Pair Encoding，字节对编码）和Unigram（Unigram Language Model，一元语言模型）是子词分词（Subword Tokenization）的两种核心算法，广泛应用于现代语言模型如BERT和GPT。BPE起源于数据压缩领域，通过迭代合并频繁字符对构建词表；Unigram则基于概率模型，选择最大化整体概率的分词方案。两者都旨在解决词汇表外（Out-of-Vocabulary, OOV）词问题，但机制不同：BPE是贪婪的、确定性的，而Unigram是概率性的、可提供多个候选。在语言建模中，这些算法帮助模型处理未见词汇，提升泛化能力。

精确定义上，BPE是一种基于频率的合并算法，核心思想是逐步将最常见字符对（character pair）合并为新token，直到达到预设词表大小。Unigram是一种语言模型分词方法，假设每个token独立，通过最大化序列概率 \( P(\mathbf{x}) = \prod_{i} P(t_i) \) 来选择分词，其中 \( t_i \) 是token，\( P(t_i) \) 从其频率估计。关键术语包括：字节对编码（Byte Pair Encoding, BPE）、一元语言模型（Unigram Language Model）、合并操作（Merge Operation）。例如，在BPE中，如果“e”和“s”频繁共现，它们可能合并为“es”。这些定义源自经典论文（来源：Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units, 2015）。

机制上，BPE算法步骤包括：初始化词表为所有字符；计算所有相邻字符对频率；合并最高频对；重复直到词表大小达标。数学上，合并准则基于频率最大化：\( \text{merge} = \arg\max_{(a,b)} \text{freq}(a,b) \)，其中 \( a \) 和 \( b \) 是字符或现有tokens。Unigram则通过动态规划求解最优分词，目标函数是 \( \max_{\mathbf{t}} \sum_{i} \log P(t_i) \)，其中 \( P(t_i) \) 通常用最大似然估计（Maximum Likelihood Estimation, MLE）从训练数据学习。Unigram还可通过退火（Annealing）调整概率，生成多样分词，如论文所述（来源：Subword Regularization: Improving Neural Network Translation Models with Multiple Subword Candidates, 2018）。

工程实现要点包括：BPE需维护频率表，复杂度为 \( O(k \cdot n) \)，其中 \( k \) 是合并次数，\( n \) 是文本长度；Unigram需预计算token概率，可能使用维特比算法（Viterbi Algorithm）进行高效解码。参数选择上，BPE的词表大小是关键，通常基于验证集性能调整；Unigram则需设置平滑参数避免零概率。在工具层面，SentencePiece库实现了两者，支持多语言。例如，训练BPE分词器时，过小的词表可能导致信息丢失，而过大会增加过拟合风险。实际中，建议从较小词表开始，逐步扩展。

常见误区包括认为BPE总是优于Unigram，或忽视算法对语言特性的适应性。失败模式可能源于训练数据偏差，如BPE在低资源语言上合并无意义对。诊断方法包括分析合并历史和比较不同参数下的分词质量。例如，如果BPE产生过多罕见tokens，可能需要调整词表大小或预处理。另一个误区是混淆BPE与WordPiece（后者类似但合并准则不同）。通过计算指标如分词一致性（Tokenization Consistency），可评估算法稳定性。实践中，混合使用BPE和Unigram可能在某些场景更优。

掌握了BPE和Unigram的原理，我们转向多语种场景，探讨如何在实际工程中应用这些算法处理复杂文本，并构建可复现的流程。

多语种分词的工程实践

多语种分词（Multilingual Tokenization）涉及处理混合语言文本，如中英文混合“Hello 世界”，需考虑语言特异性、字符编码和模型兼容性。随着全球化应用增多，如机器翻译或跨语言检索，高效的多语言分词成为关键。挑战包括语言识别（Language Identification）、处理不同书写系统（如拉丁字母vs.汉字）和平衡词表大小。例如，中文通常按字符分词，而英文可能用BPE，混合时需协调策略。这要求工程师理解Unicode编码和语言检测技术。

精确定义上，多语种分词指为多种语言设计统一或混合的分词流程。关键术语包括：Unicode（统一字符编码标准）、语言标识（Language Identification）、特殊token（Special Tokens，如[CLS]、[SEP]）。例如，在Transformer模型中，特殊token用于分隔序列或表示任务。数学上，多语言分词可视为一个优化问题：最小化整体困惑度（Perplexity）或最大化跨语言对齐（Cross-lingual Alignment）。评估指标常用双语评估替分（BLEU, Bilingual Evaluation Understudy），但针对分词，可使用token重叠率（Token Overlap Rate）：\( \text{TOR} = \frac{|\text{tokens}_1 \cap \text{tokens}_2|}{\max(|\text{tokens}_1|, |\text{tokens}_2|)} \)，比较不同分词器的输出一致性。

机制上，多语种分词流程包括：文本预处理（统一为UTF-8编码）、语言检测（可用库如langdetect）、应用语言特定分词器、后处理（如添加特殊token）。工程实现要点是使用灵活的工具如SentencePiece，它支持从混合语料训练单一分词器，通过Unicode编码处理多语言。例如，SentencePiece将文本视为Unicode字符序列，无需预先分词，从而支持无空格语言。复杂度方面，语言检测增加 \( O(n) \) 开销，但可缓存结果优化。根据官方文档（来源：SentencePiece GitHub Repository），该工具简化了多语言处理。

在实现中，关键步骤是训练分词器：收集多语言数据、清洗（去除噪声）、训练BPE或Unigram模型。例如，为处理中英文，可混合使用中文维基百科和英文新闻数据。失败模式可能源于编码错误（如非UTF-8字符）或语言误判，导致分词错误。诊断方法包括检查token分布按语言和可视化分词边界。另一个常见误区是假设一个词表适用于所有语言；实际上，不同语言可能需要不同粒度，如中文字符vs.英文子词。通过以下综合示例，我们构建一个可复现的多语言分词流程，应用BPE和Unigram，并计算评估指标以巩固理解。

import sentencepiece as spm
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

# Step 1: Construct mixed Chinese-English text data (inline, no external files)
texts = [
    "Hello world",
    "你好世界",
    "Hello 世界",
    "Natural Language Processing 自然语言处理",
    "Tokenization is a fundamental step"
]
print("Original text examples:")
for t in texts[:3]:
    print(f"  {t}")
print(f"Data scale: {len(texts)} texts")

# Step 2: Text cleaning (simple removal of extra spaces, may need more in practice)
cleaned_texts = [t.strip() for t in texts]

# Step 3: Train BPE tokenizer (using inline data, avoiding temporary files)
corpus_text = '\n'.join(cleaned_texts)
spm.SentencePieceTrainer.train(
    sentence_iterator=iter([corpus_text]),
    model_prefix='bpe_model',
    vocab_size=50,  # Small vocabulary for demonstration
    model_type='bpe',
    input_format='text'
)
sp_bpe = spm.SentencePieceProcessor(model_file='bpe_model.model')

# Train Unigram tokenizer
spm.SentencePieceTrainer.train(
    sentence_iterator=iter([corpus_text]),
    model_prefix='unigram_model',
    vocab_size=50,
    model_type='unigram',
    input_format='text'
)
sp_uni = spm.SentencePieceProcessor(model_file='unigram_model.model')

print(f"BPE vocabulary size: {sp_bpe.get_piece_size()}")
print(f"Unigram vocabulary size: {sp_uni.get_piece_size()}")

# Step 4: Apply tokenizers to new text
sample_text = "Hello 世界 Tokenization"
tokens_bpe = sp_bpe.encode_as_pieces(sample_text)
tokens_uni = sp_uni.encode_as_pieces(sample_text)
print(f"Sample text: {sample_text}")
print(f"BPE tokenization result: {tokens_bpe}")
print(f"Unigram tokenization result: {tokens_uni}")

# Step 5: Compute evaluation metric - Token Overlap Rate (TOR)
def token_overlap_rate(tokens1, tokens2):
    set1, set2 = set(tokens1), set(tokens2)
    overlap = len(set1.intersection(set2))
    max_len = max(len(set1), len(set2))
    return overlap / max_len if max_len > 0 else 0.0

tor = token_overlap_rate(tokens_bpe, tokens_uni)
print(f"Token Overlap Rate (TOR) between BPE and Unigram: {tor:.3f}")
print("Formula: TOR = |tokens1 ∩ tokens2| / max(|tokens1|, |tokens2|)")

# Print intermediate variables
print(f"BPE token sequence length: {len(tokens_bpe)}")
print(f"Unigram token sequence length: {len(tokens_uni)}")

# Clean up temporary files
import os
if os.path.exists('bpe_model.model'):
    os.remove('bpe_model.model')
if os.path.exists('bpe_model.vocab'):
    os.remove('bpe_model.vocab')
if os.path.exists('unigram_model.model'):
    os.remove('unigram_model.model')
if os.path.exists('unigram_model.vocab'):
    os.remove('unigram_model.vocab')

此示例展示了端到端流程：从内联数据构造、清洗、训练BPE和Unigram分词器，到应用和评估。输出包括原始文本、词表大小、分词结果和TOR指标。TOR计算了两种算法分词结果的重叠程度，值越高表示一致性越好；这里TOR较低，反映BPE和Unigram在不同语言上的策略差异。通过调整vocab_size或添加更多数据，可优化分词效果。此代码完全可复现，无需外部文件，依赖仅sentencepiece。轻量替代方案：若无法安装sentencepiece，可用简单规则分词（如按空格和字符分割）作为baseline，但会损失子词优势。

总结来说，分词是语言模型的基石，BPE和Unigram提供了灵活的子词解决方案，而多语种处理需结合语言特性和工程实践。掌握这些概念，您能更有效地设计提示和理解模型行为，为高级NLP任务打下基础。
content.en:
From Characters to Tokens: Why Tokenization Matters

In natural language processing (NLP), language models (LMs) cannot directly process raw text strings. Text consists of character sequences, but characters themselves lack semantic information. For example, the English word "unhappiness" contains 13 characters, but a model needs to understand it as a combination of "un-" (negation prefix), "happi" (stem), and "-ness" (noun suffix). Tokenization is the process of converting continuous text into discrete units called tokens, which can be words, subwords, or characters, forming the foundation of model input. In large language models (LLMs) like the GPT series, tokenization determines how the model "sees" text, directly impacting its comprehension and generation capabilities. This step is fundamental to language modeling, especially in prompt engineering, where token count relates directly to context window limits.

Precisely defined, tokenization refers to the algorithm or pipeline that segments text into tokens. Key terms include: Tokenization, Subword (text units between characters and full words), and Vocabulary (the set of all possible tokens). For instance, in Chinese, "自然语言处理" might be tokenized into ["自然", "语言", "处理"], while in subword tokenization, English "lower" might be decomposed into ["low", "er"]. The goal of tokenization is to balance vocabulary size and semantic granularity: an overly large vocabulary leads to sparsity issues, while an overly small one loses semantic detail. Mathematically, tokenization can be viewed as a mapping function \( f: T \rightarrow V \), where \( T \) is the text space and \( V \) is the vocabulary index space, aiming to maximize compression efficiency or language model probability.

Mechanistically, the core of tokenization is selecting an appropriate segmentation strategy. Traditional methods like whitespace tokenization are simple but limited, unable to handle languages without spaces (e.g., Chinese) or compound words (e.g., "New York"). More advanced methods are based on statistics or neural networks, such as BPE (Byte Pair Encoding) and Unigram (Unigram Language Model). Common metrics for evaluating tokenization quality include compression ratio, defined as the ratio of original text length to token count: \( CR = \frac{L_{\text{text}}}{N_{\text{tokens}}} \), where \( L_{\text{text}} \) is the character count and \( N_{\text{tokens}} \) is the token count. A high compression ratio indicates more efficient representation but may sacrifice semantics. Another key metric is vocabulary coverage, measuring the proportion of different text units in training data covered by the vocabulary.

In engineering implementation, the tokenization pipeline includes text preprocessing (e.g., normalization, removing special characters), applying tokenization algorithms, and vocabulary construction. A key point is that handling multilingual text requires unified encoding (e.g., UTF-8) and consideration of language specificity. For example, English might use BPE, while Chinese might be segmented by characters or words. In terms of complexity, tokenization is typically \( O(n) \) linear time, but vocabulary size affects memory usage. Latency-sensitive aspects include tokenizer initialization and batch processing optimization. In prompt engineering, tokenization influences prompt length calculation, e.g., GPT-3's context window is measured in tokens, not characters, requiring engineers to precisely control input scale.

Common misconceptions include thinking tokenization is merely splitting by spaces, or that one vocabulary can handle all languages. Failure modes may arise from not handling rare characters or encoding errors, leading to noisy model input. Diagnostic methods include checking token distributions (e.g., frequency histograms) and comparing outputs from different tokenizers. For instance, if the token count is abnormally high, it may indicate over-segmentation. Another misconception is neglecting the indirect impact of tokenization on model performance, such as increased training costs with large vocabularies. By visualizing token sequences and computing metrics like vocabulary coverage, one can assess tokenization effectiveness. In practice, using standardized tools like SentencePiece (source: SentencePiece: A simple and language independent subword tokenizer and detokenizer for Neural Text Processing, 2018) helps avoid common pitfalls.

Understanding the foundational role and challenges of tokenization, we now delve into two mainstream algorithms: BPE and Unigram, which optimize the tokenization process from different angles and lay the groundwork for multilingual handling.

BPE and Unigram: Core Ideas of Two Subword Algorithms

BPE (Byte Pair Encoding) and Unigram (Unigram Language Model) are two core algorithms for subword tokenization, widely used in modern language models like BERT and GPT. BPE originates from data compression, building vocabularies by iteratively merging frequent character pairs; Unigram is based on a probabilistic model, selecting segmentation that maximizes overall probability. Both aim to address out-of-vocabulary (OOV) word issues, but their mechanisms differ: BPE is greedy and deterministic, while Unigram is probabilistic and can provide multiple candidates. In language modeling, these algorithms help models handle unseen vocabulary, improving generalization.

Precisely defined, BPE is a frequency-based merging algorithm whose core idea is to gradually merge the most common character pairs into new tokens until a preset vocabulary size is reached. Unigram is a language model tokenization method that assumes each token is independent, selecting segmentation by maximizing sequence probability \( P(\mathbf{x}) = \prod_{i} P(t_i) \), where \( t_i \) is a token and \( P(t_i) \) is estimated from its frequency. Key terms include: Byte Pair Encoding (BPE), Unigram Language Model, and Merge Operation. For example, in BPE, if "e" and "s" co-occur frequently, they might merge into "es". These definitions stem from classic papers (source: Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units, 2015).

Mechanistically, the BPE algorithm steps include: initializing the vocabulary with all characters; computing frequencies of all adjacent character pairs; merging the highest-frequency pair; repeating until vocabulary size is met. Mathematically, the merging criterion is based on frequency maximization: \( \text{merge} = \arg\max_{(a,b)} \text{freq}(a,b) \), where \( a \) and \( b \) are characters or existing tokens. Unigram solves for optimal segmentation via dynamic programming, with the objective function \( \max_{\mathbf{t}} \sum_{i} \log P(t_i) \), where \( P(t_i) \) is typically learned from training data using maximum likelihood estimation (MLE). Unigram can also adjust probabilities through annealing to generate diverse segmentations, as described in papers (source: Subword Regularization: Improving Neural Network Translation Models with Multiple Subword Candidates, 2018).

Engineering implementation points include: BPE requires maintaining a frequency table, with complexity \( O(k \cdot n) \), where \( k \) is the number of merges and \( n \) is text length; Unigram needs precomputed token probabilities, possibly using the Viterbi algorithm for efficient decoding. In parameter selection, BPE's vocabulary size is critical, usually tuned based on validation set performance; Unigram requires smoothing parameters to avoid zero probabilities. At the tool level, the SentencePiece library implements both, supporting multiple languages. For example, when training a BPE tokenizer, too small a vocabulary may lose information, while too large increases overfitting risk. In practice, starting with a smaller vocabulary and gradually expanding is recommended.

Common misconceptions include thinking BPE is always better than Unigram, or ignoring algorithm adaptability to language characteristics. Failure modes may stem from training data bias, e.g., BPE merging meaningless pairs in low-resource languages. Diagnostic methods include analyzing merge histories and comparing segmentation quality under different parameters. For instance, if BPE produces too many rare tokens, adjusting vocabulary size or preprocessing may be needed. Another misconception is confusing BPE with WordPiece (the latter is similar but has a different merging criterion). By computing metrics like tokenization consistency, one can evaluate algorithm stability. In practice, hybrid use of BPE and Unigram may be optimal in certain scenarios.

Having grasped the principles of BPE and Unigram, we turn to multilingual scenarios, exploring how to apply these algorithms in practical engineering to handle complex texts and build reproducible pipelines.

Engineering Practices for Multilingual Tokenization

Multilingual tokenization involves processing mixed-language texts, such as Chinese-English "Hello 世界", requiring consideration of language specificity, character encoding, and model compatibility. With the rise of global applications like machine translation or cross-lingual retrieval, efficient multilingual tokenization becomes crucial. Challenges include language identification, handling different writing systems (e.g., Latin alphabet vs. Chinese characters), and balancing vocabulary sizes. For example, Chinese is often tokenized by characters, while English might use BPE, necessitating coordinated strategies for mixtures. This requires engineers to understand Unicode encoding and language detection techniques.

Precisely defined, multilingual tokenization refers to designing unified or hybrid tokenization pipelines for multiple languages. Key terms include: Unicode (the universal character encoding standard), Language Identification, and Special Tokens (e.g., [CLS], [SEP]). For instance, in Transformer models, special tokens are used to separate sequences or represent tasks. Mathematically, multilingual tokenization can be viewed as an optimization problem: minimizing overall perplexity or maximizing cross-lingual alignment. Common evaluation metrics include BLEU (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy), but for tokenization, token overlap rate can be used: \( \text{TOR} = \frac{|\text{tokens}_1 \cap \text{tokens}_2|}{\max(|\text{tokens}_1|, |\text{tokens}_2|)} \), comparing output consistency across tokenizers.

Mechanistically, the multilingual tokenization pipeline includes: text preprocessing (unifying to UTF-8 encoding), language detection (using libraries like langdetect), applying language-specific tokenizers, and post-processing (e.g., adding special tokens). An engineering key point is using flexible tools like SentencePiece, which supports training a single tokenizer from mixed corpora, handling multiple languages via Unicode encoding. For example, SentencePiece treats text as Unicode character sequences, requiring no pre-tokenization, thus supporting languages without spaces. In terms of complexity, language detection adds \( O(n) \) overhead but can be optimized by caching results. According to official documentation (source: SentencePiece GitHub Repository), this tool simplifies multilingual processing.

In implementation, a key step is training the tokenizer: collecting multilingual data, cleaning (removing noise), and training BPE or Unigram models. For instance, to handle Chinese-English, one might mix Chinese Wikipedia and English news data. Failure modes may arise from encoding errors (e.g., non-UTF-8 characters) or language misidentification, leading to incorrect tokenization. Diagnostic methods include checking token distributions by language and visualizing segmentation boundaries. Another common misconception is assuming one vocabulary suits all languages; in reality, different languages may require different granularities, such as Chinese characters vs. English subwords. Through the following comprehensive example, we build a reproducible multilingual tokenization pipeline, applying BPE and Unigram, and compute evaluation metrics to solidify understanding.

import sentencepiece as spm
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

# Step 1: Construct mixed Chinese-English text data (inline, no external files)
texts = [
    "Hello world",
    "你好世界",
    "Hello 世界",
    "Natural Language Processing 自然语言处理",
    "Tokenization is a fundamental step"
]
print("Original text examples:")
for t in texts[:3]:
    print(f"  {t}")
print(f"Data scale: {len(texts)} texts")

# Step 2: Text cleaning (simple removal of extra spaces, may need more in practice)
cleaned_texts = [t.strip() for t in texts]

# Step 3: Train BPE tokenizer (using inline data, avoiding temporary files)
corpus_text = '\n'.join(cleaned_texts)
spm.SentencePieceTrainer.train(
    sentence_iterator=iter([corpus_text]),
    model_prefix='bpe_model',
    vocab_size=50,  # Small vocabulary for demonstration
    model_type='bpe',
    input_format='text'
)
sp_bpe = spm.SentencePieceProcessor(model_file='bpe_model.model')

# Train Unigram tokenizer
spm.SentencePieceTrainer.train(
    sentence_iterator=iter([corpus_text]),
    model_prefix='unigram_model',
    vocab_size=50,
    model_type='unigram',
    input_format='text'
)
sp_uni = spm.SentencePieceProcessor(model_file='unigram_model.model')

print(f"BPE vocabulary size: {sp_bpe.get_piece_size()}")
print(f"Unigram vocabulary size: {sp_uni.get_piece_size()}")

# Step 4: Apply tokenizers to new text
sample_text = "Hello 世界 Tokenization"
tokens_bpe = sp_bpe.encode_as_pieces(sample_text)
tokens_uni = sp_uni.encode_as_pieces(sample_text)
print(f"Sample text: {sample_text}")
print(f"BPE tokenization result: {tokens_bpe}")
print(f"Unigram tokenization result: {tokens_uni}")

# Step 5: Compute evaluation metric - Token Overlap Rate (TOR)
def token_overlap_rate(tokens1, tokens2):
    set1, set2 = set(tokens1), set(tokens2)
    overlap = len(set1.intersection(set2))
    max_len = max(len(set1), len(set2))
    return overlap / max_len if max_len > 0 else 0.0

tor = token_overlap_rate(tokens_bpe, tokens_uni)
print(f"Token Overlap Rate (TOR) between BPE and Unigram: {tor:.3f}")
print("Formula: TOR = |tokens1 ∩ tokens2| / max(|tokens1|, |tokens2|)")

# Print intermediate variables
print(f"BPE token sequence length: {len(tokens_bpe)}")
print(f"Unigram token sequence length: {len(tokens_uni)}")

# Clean up temporary files
import os
if os.path.exists('bpe_model.model'):
    os.remove('bpe_model.model')
if os.path.exists('bpe_model.vocab'):
    os.remove('bpe_model.vocab')
if os.path.exists('unigram_model.model'):
    os.remove('unigram_model.model')
if os.path.exists('unigram_model.vocab'):
    os.remove('unigram_model.vocab')

This example demonstrates an end-to-end pipeline: from inline data construction, cleaning, training BPE and Unigram tokenizers, to application and evaluation. Outputs include original texts, vocabulary sizes, tokenization results, and the TOR metric. TOR calculates the overlap between tokenization results from the two algorithms, with higher values indicating better consistency; here, a low TOR reflects strategic differences between BPE and Unigram across languages. By adjusting vocab_size or adding more data, tokenization can be optimized. This code is fully reproducible, requiring no external files and dependencies only on sentencepiece. Lightweight alternative: if sentencepiece cannot be installed, simple rule-based tokenization (e.g., splitting by spaces and characters) can serve as a baseline, but loses subword advantages.

In summary, tokenization is the cornerstone of language models, with BPE and Unigram offering flexible subword solutions, while multilingual handling requires combining language characteristics and engineering practices. Mastering these concepts enables more effective prompt design and model behavior understanding, laying a foundation for advanced NLP tasks.

summary.zh: 本课程系统梳理自然语言处理四大核心任务：分类、序列标注、生成与评测。通过数学形式化定义、机制解释与工程实践，建立从传统方法到大语言模型应用的可执行知识框架。课程涵盖交叉熵损失、条件随机场、自回归生成等关键数学模型，提供TF-IDF+逻辑回归的完整可复现代码示例，并强调可复现性、评估指标多维分析与常见误区诊断。学习者将掌握根据具体需求选择技术路径的系统方法。
summary.en: This course systematically organizes four core natural language processing tasks: classification, sequence labeling, generation, and evaluation. Through mathematical formalization, mechanism explanation, and engineering practice, it establishes an executable knowledge framework from traditional methods to large language model applications. The course covers key mathematical models including cross-entropy loss, conditional random fields, and autoregressive generation, provides a complete reproducible code example of TF-IDF + logistic regression, and emphasizes reproducibility, multi-dimensional evaluation metric analysis, and common misconception diagnosis. Learners will master systematic methods for selecting technical paths based on specific needs.

content.zh:
从直觉到定义：为什么需要NLP任务地图

面对海量文本数据时，工程师常陷入“不知从何下手”的困境。是直接调用大语言模型API，还是构建传统机器学习管线？这种选择困惑源于缺乏对自然语言处理任务体系的系统认知。NLP任务地图（NLP Task Map）正是为解决这一问题而设计的分类框架，它将复杂多样的文本处理需求归纳为四大核心任务：分类（Classification）、序列标注（Sequence Labeling）、生成（Generation）与评测（Evaluation）。每个任务都有其独特的数学形式化定义、实现机制和适用场景。

分类任务为文本分配预定义类别标签，其数学本质是学习从文本特征空间到离散标签空间的映射函数。给定文本序列 \(x = (w_1, w_2, ..., w_n)\)，分类模型需要预测其所属类别 \(y \in \{1, 2, ..., K\}\)，其中K为类别总数。目标函数通常采用交叉熵损失：\[\mathcal{L}_{CE} = -\sum_{i=1}^{K} y_i \log(\hat{y}_i)\]，其中\(y_i\)为真实标签的one-hot编码，\(\hat{y}_i\)为模型预测的概率分布。这个公式直观反映了预测概率与真实分布之间的差异。

工程实现时，分类任务的数据流遵循“原始文本→特征提取→分类器→评估”的标准管线。特征提取阶段，传统方法常用TF-IDF（词频-逆文档频率）将文本转换为数值向量：\[\text{TF-IDF}(t,d) = \text{TF}(t,d) \times \log\frac{N}{\text{DF}(t)}\]，其中t为词项，d为文档，N为文档总数，DF(t)为包含词项t的文档数。现代深度学习方法则使用预训练语言模型（如BERT）的[CLS] token表示作为特征。延迟敏感点主要在于特征提取的计算复杂度，TF-IDF为O(n·m)，而BERT推理为O(n²·d)，其中n为序列长度，m为词汇表大小，d为隐藏层维度。

常见误区是认为“大语言模型可以解决所有分类任务”。实际上，传统方法在特定场景仍有优势：当训练数据规模较小（<1000样本）时，逻辑回归等简单模型往往比微调大模型更稳定；当推理延迟要求极严格（<10ms）时，TF-IDF+线性分类器的组合远快于大模型推理；当需要完全可控的决策边界时，传统模型的参数可解释性更强。失败模式包括类别不平衡导致的模型偏向、特征稀疏导致的过拟合、以及测试集泄露造成的虚假高准确率。

诊断分类模型问题时，应同时查看多个评估指标。准确率\(\text{Accuracy} = \frac{TP+TN}{TP+TN+FP+FN}\)仅适用于类别平衡的数据集；对于不平衡数据，需要结合精确率\(\text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP+FP}\)、召回率\(\text{Recall} = \frac{TP}{TP+FN}\)和F1分数\(\text{F1} = 2 \times \frac{\text{Precision} \times \text{Recall}}{\text{Precision} + \text{Recall}}\)进行综合评估。混淆矩阵可视化能清晰展示各类别的错分模式。

理解了分类任务的定义与边界后，我们自然会问：当标签需要分配给序列中的每个token而非整个文本时，该如何处理？这引出了序列标注任务的独特挑战。

任务机制详解：从传统方法到提示工程

序列标注任务要求为文本序列中的每个token分配标签，典型应用包括命名实体识别、词性标注和语义角色标注。与分类任务不同，序列标注需要考虑token之间的上下文依赖关系。数学上，给定输入序列\(x = (x_1, x_2, ..., x_T)\)，模型需要输出标签序列\(y = (y_1, y_2, ..., y_T)\)，其中每个\(y_t \in \mathcal{Y}\)来自有限的标签集。条件随机场（CRF）是传统序列标注的核心模型，其目标函数为：\[P(y|x) = \frac{1}{Z(x)} \exp\left(\sum_{t=1}^{T} \sum_{k=1}^{K} \theta_k f_k(y_t, y_{t-1}, x, t)\right)\]，其中\(Z(x)\)为归一化因子，\(f_k\)为特征函数，\(\theta_k\)为可学习参数。

现代深度学习方法用神经网络替代手工特征工程。双向LSTM-CRF架构通过LSTM层捕获上下文信息，CRF层确保标签序列的全局一致性。Transformer架构（来源：Attention Is All You Need, 2017）引入自注意力机制，允许每个token直接关注序列中的所有其他token，计算复杂度为O(T²·d)。预训练语言模型BERT（来源：BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding, 2019）通过掩码语言建模任务学习丰富的上下文表示，微调时只需在顶层添加线性分类器即可用于序列标注。

工程实现要点包括：数据标注需遵循BIO或BIOES等标注规范；批处理时需处理变长序列（常用padding和masking）；评估时需按token而非样本计算指标。对于命名实体识别，常用指标包括实体级别的精确率、召回率和F1分数。序列标注对计算资源敏感，长序列（>512 token）需要分段处理或使用长上下文模型。

常见误区是“序列标注就是为每个词独立分类”。实际上，标签之间存在强依赖关系：在命名实体识别中，“B-LOC”后应接“I-LOC”而非“B-PER”；在词性标注中，冠词后通常接名词而非动词。忽略这些约束会导致不合法的标签序列。另一个误区是过度依赖大模型，对于领域特定的实体类型（如医疗术语、法律条款），基于规则或词典的方法可能更准确且高效。

失败模式包括：标注不一致导致的训练噪声、罕见实体召回率低、嵌套实体识别困难。诊断时，应分析混淆矩阵中特定实体类型的错分模式，检查边界识别错误（B/I标签混淆）还是类型识别错误（LOC/ORG混淆）。对于长实体，可计算边界精确率（边界完全匹配的比例）。

掌握了离散标签的分配机制后，我们转向更具创造性的任务：如何让模型生成连贯、相关、多样化的文本？这需要深入理解文本生成的概率建模本质。

工程实践：构建可复现的NLP任务管线

文本生成任务要求模型根据输入生成连贯的文本输出，涵盖机器翻译、摘要生成、对话系统等应用。数学上，生成模型需要建模条件概率分布\(P(y|x)\)，其中\(y = (y_1, y_2, ..., y_M)\)为输出序列。自回归生成通过链式法则分解该概率：\[P(y|x) = \prod_{t=1}^{M} P(y_t | y_{<t}, x)\]，每个时间步基于已生成前缀和输入预测下一个token。目标函数为负对数似然：\[\mathcal{L}_{NLL} = -\sum_{t=1}^{M} \log P(y_t | y_{<t}, x)\]。

传统统计方法如n-gram语言模型基于马尔可夫假设，仅考虑有限历史上下文。神经生成模型使用RNN、LSTM或Transformer编码输入并解码输出。现代大语言模型通过提示工程（Prompt Engineering）引导生成：设计提示模板\(\text{prompt}(x)\)，让模型补全后续文本。例如，摘要生成提示可为“请为以下文章生成摘要：{文章内容}\n摘要：”。提示工程的核心是找到能激发模型相关知识的表达方式，同时控制生成风格和格式。

评测生成质量是核心挑战。自动评测指标ROUGE（Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation）基于n-gram重叠度计算：\[\text{ROUGE-N} = \frac{\sum_{S\in\{\text{参考摘要}\}} \sum_{\text{gram}_n\in S} \text{Count}_{\text{match}}(\text{gram}_n)}{\sum_{S\in\{\text{参考摘要}\}} \sum_{\text{gram}_n\in S} \text{Count}(\text{gram}_n)}\]，其中N为n-gram长度，\(\text{Count}_{\text{match}}\)为生成摘要与参考摘要共享的n-gram数量。ROUGE-1关注unigram重叠，ROUGE-2关注bigram重叠，ROUGE-L关注最长公共子序列。

工程实现需确保可复现性：固定随机种子、记录依赖包版本、保存中间结果。数据管线应包括清洗（去除HTML标签、标准化空格）、分词（按任务选择词、字或子词单元）、划分（按stratify方式保持类别分布）。模型训练需监控训练/验证损失曲线，防止过拟合。部署时需考虑生成速度（受解码算法和序列长度影响）和内存占用（模型参数量）。

常见误区是“准确率高就代表模型好”。对于生成任务，高ROUGE分数可能对应流畅但无关的文本，或相关但冗余的文本。需要结合人工评估检查生成内容的忠实度（是否歪曲原意）、连贯性（是否逻辑通顺）和信息量（是否包含关键信息）。另一个误区是忽视提示工程的系统性：提示应经过A/B测试优化，记录不同模板的性能差异。

失败模式包括：生成重复内容（因beam search的多样性不足）、生成无关内容（因注意力机制失效）、生成不安全内容（因训练数据偏见）。诊断时，应分析生成样本的错误类型，调整解码参数（如temperature、top-p）、修改提示模板、或增加后处理规则。对于关键应用，应建立回归测试集，监控模型更新后的性能变化。

现在，让我们将这些理论知识落实到具体代码中，构建一个完整的文本分类系统，体验从数据到评估的全流程。

可复现示例：新闻文本分类系统

以下代码构建了一个端到端的新闻文本分类系统，使用scikit-learn内置的20newsgroups数据集（来源：Scikit-learn: Machine Learning in Python, 2011）。我们实现TF-IDF特征提取+逻辑回归的完整管线，计算准确率和F1分数，并可视化混淆矩阵进行错误分析。

# 代码块#1：端到端新闻文本分类系统
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.datasets import fetch_20newsgroups
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, f1_score, confusion_matrix
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

# 固定随机种子确保可复现性
np.random.seed(42)

# 1. 加载数据集并检查基本信息
data = fetch_20newsgroups(subset='all', remove=('headers', 'footers', 'quotes'))
print(f"数据集shape: {len(data.data)} samples, {len(data.target_names)} categories")
print(f"前3个类别: {data.target_names[:3]}")
print(f"样例文本（前200字符）: {data.data[0][:200]}...")
print(f"对应标签: {data.target_names[data.target[0]]}")

# 2. 划分训练集、验证集、测试集（stratify保持类别分布）
X_temp, X_test, y_temp, y_test = train_test_split(
    data.data, data.target, test_size=0.2, random_state=42, stratify=data.target
)
X_train, X_val, y_train, y_val = train_test_split(
    X_temp, y_temp, test_size=0.25, random_state=42, stratify=y_temp  # 0.25 * 0.8 = 0.2
)
print(f"训练集: {len(X_train)} samples, 验证集: {len(X_val)} samples, 测试集: {len(X_test)} samples")

# 3. 构建TF-IDF + 逻辑回归pipeline
pipeline = Pipeline([
    ('tfidf', TfidfVectorizer(max_features=10000, stop_words='english')),
    ('clf', LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, random_state=42))
])

# 训练模型
pipeline.fit(X_train, y_train)

# 4. 评估模型
val_pred = pipeline.predict(X_val)
val_accuracy = accuracy_score(y_val, val_pred)
val_f1 = f1_score(y_val, val_pred, average='macro')
print(f"验证集准确率: {val_accuracy:.4f}")
print(f"验证集宏平均F1分数: {val_f1:.4f}")

# 在测试集上最终评估
test_pred = pipeline.predict(X_test)
test_accuracy = accuracy_score(y_test, test_pred)
test_f1 = f1_score(y_test, test_pred, average='macro')
print(f"测试集准确率: {test_accuracy:.4f}")
print(f"测试集宏平均F1分数: {test_f1:.4f}")

# 5. 混淆矩阵可视化
cm = confusion_matrix(y_test, test_pred)
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 10))
sns.heatmap(cm, annot=True, fmt='d', cmap='Blues', 
            xticklabels=data.target_names, yticklabels=data.target_names)
plt.title('Confusion Matrix for 20 Newsgroups Classification')
plt.xlabel('Predicted Label')
plt.ylabel('True Label')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# 6. 错误分析：找出最易混淆的类别对
confusion_pairs = []
for i in range(len(data.target_names)):
    for j in range(len(data.target_names)):
        if i != j and cm[i, j] > 5:  # 忽略少量错分
            confusion_pairs.append((data.target_names[i], data.target_names[j], cm[i, j]))
confusion_pairs.sort(key=lambda x: x[2], reverse=True)
print("\n最易混淆的类别对（错分样本数>5）:")
for true_label, pred_label, count in confusion_pairs[:5]:
    print(f"  {true_label} → {pred_label}: {count} samples")

# 7. 记录关键信息
print("\n关键依赖包版本:")
import sklearn
print(f"scikit-learn: {sklearn.__version__}")
print(f"numpy: {np.__version__}")
print(f"随机种子: 42")

运行此代码将输出数据集规模、类别数量、样例文本，并计算测试集准确率和宏平均F1分数。混淆矩阵可视化展示各类别的错分模式，错误分析识别最易混淆的类别对（如“comp.sys.ibm.pc.hardware”与“comp.sys.mac.hardware”）。该实现完全自包含，无需外部数据文件，可在任何配置了scikit-learn的环境中复现。

若需替换为深度学习模型，可将TF-IDF向量器替换为BERT特征提取器：使用transformers库加载预训练BERT模型，提取[CLS] token的隐藏状态作为特征，然后输入相同的逻辑回归分类器。注意深度模型需要GPU加速，且推理延迟显著高于传统方法。

通过本课程，我们系统梳理了NLP四大核心任务的定义、机制与工程实践。分类任务学习离散标签映射，序列标注建模token级依赖，生成任务自回归预测序列，评测任务量化模型性能。每种任务都有其适用的数学工具、实现要点和评估标准。掌握这张任务地图，你便能根据具体需求选择合适的技术路径，无论是构建传统机器学习管线还是设计大语言模型提示。下一步，可探索检索增强生成（RAG）如何结合检索与生成任务，或深入研究LLM评估指标的设计原理。
content.en:
From Intuition to Definition: Why We Need an NLP Task Map

When confronted with massive text data, engineers often face the dilemma of "not knowing where to start." Should they directly call large language model APIs or build traditional machine learning pipelines? This confusion stems from a lack of systematic understanding of the natural language processing task landscape. The NLP Task Map is designed to address this issue—a classification framework that organizes diverse text processing needs into four core tasks: classification, sequence labeling, generation, and evaluation. Each task has its unique mathematical formalization, implementation mechanisms, and applicable scenarios.

Classification tasks assign predefined category labels to texts, mathematically learning a mapping function from text feature space to discrete label space. Given a text sequence \(x = (w_1, w_2, ..., w_n)\), the classification model predicts its category \(y \in \{1, 2, ..., K\}\), where K is the total number of categories. The objective function typically uses cross-entropy loss: \[\mathcal{L}_{CE} = -\sum_{i=1}^{K} y_i \log(\hat{y}_i)\] where \(y_i\) is the one-hot encoding of the true label and \(\hat{y}_i\) is the model's predicted probability distribution. This formula intuitively reflects the discrepancy between predicted probabilities and the true distribution.

In engineering implementation, classification tasks follow a standard pipeline: "raw text → feature extraction → classifier → evaluation." For feature extraction, traditional methods often use TF-IDF (Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency) to convert text into numerical vectors: \[\text{TF-IDF}(t,d) = \text{TF}(t,d) \times \log\frac{N}{\text{DF}(t)}\] where t is a term, d is a document, N is the total number of documents, and DF(t) is the number of documents containing term t. Modern deep learning approaches use the [CLS] token representation from pre-trained language models (e.g., BERT) as features. Latency-sensitive points mainly involve the computational complexity of feature extraction: O(n·m) for TF-IDF versus O(n²·d) for BERT inference, where n is sequence length, m is vocabulary size, and d is hidden dimension.

A common misconception is that "large language models can solve all classification tasks." In reality, traditional methods still have advantages in specific scenarios: when training data is small (<1000 samples), simple models like logistic regression are often more stable than fine-tuning large models; when inference latency requirements are extremely strict (<10ms), TF-IDF + linear classifier combinations are much faster than large model inference; when fully controllable decision boundaries are needed, traditional models offer better parameter interpretability. Failure modes include model bias due to class imbalance, overfitting from sparse features, and inflated accuracy from test set leakage.

To diagnose classification model issues, multiple evaluation metrics should be examined simultaneously. Accuracy \(\text{Accuracy} = \frac{TP+TN}{TP+TN+FP+FN}\) is only suitable for balanced datasets; for imbalanced data, precision \(\text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP+FP}\), recall \(\text{Recall} = \frac{TP}{TP+FN}\), and F1-score \(\text{F1} = 2 \times \frac{\text{Precision} \times \text{Recall}}{\text{Precision} + \text{Recall}}\) should be combined for comprehensive assessment. Confusion matrix visualization clearly displays misclassification patterns across categories.

After understanding the definition and boundaries of classification tasks, a natural question arises: when labels need to be assigned to each token in a sequence rather than the entire text, how should we proceed? This leads to the unique challenges of sequence labeling tasks.

Task Mechanism Deep Dive: From Traditional Methods to Prompt Engineering

Sequence labeling tasks require assigning labels to each token in a text sequence, with typical applications including named entity recognition, part-of-speech tagging, and semantic role labeling. Unlike classification tasks, sequence labeling must consider contextual dependencies between tokens. Mathematically, given an input sequence \(x = (x_1, x_2, ..., x_T)\), the model outputs a label sequence \(y = (y_1, y_2, ..., y_T)\), where each \(y_t \in \mathcal{Y}\) comes from a finite label set. Conditional Random Fields (CRF) are core traditional models for sequence labeling, with objective function: \[P(y|x) = \frac{1}{Z(x)} \exp\left(\sum_{t=1}^{T} \sum_{k=1}^{K} \theta_k f_k(y_t, y_{t-1}, x, t)\right)\] where \(Z(x)\) is the normalization factor, \(f_k\) are feature functions, and \(\theta_k\) are learnable parameters.

Modern deep learning methods replace manual feature engineering with neural networks. The BiLSTM-CRF architecture uses LSTM layers to capture contextual information, with a CRF layer ensuring global consistency of label sequences. The Transformer architecture (Source: Attention Is All You Need, 2017) introduces self-attention mechanisms, allowing each token to directly attend to all other tokens in the sequence, with computational complexity O(T²·d). Pre-trained language model BERT (Source: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding, 2019) learns rich contextual representations through masked language modeling tasks; fine-tuning only requires adding a linear classifier on top for sequence labeling.

Engineering implementation points include: data annotation should follow labeling schemes like BIO or BIOES; batch processing must handle variable-length sequences (commonly using padding and masking); evaluation should compute metrics per token rather than per sample. For named entity recognition, common metrics include entity-level precision, recall, and F1-score. Sequence labeling is sensitive to computational resources; long sequences (>512 tokens) require segmentation or long-context models.

A common misconception is that "sequence labeling is just independent classification for each word." In reality, strong dependencies exist between labels: in named entity recognition, "B-LOC" should be followed by "I-LOC" not "B-PER"; in part-of-speech tagging, articles are typically followed by nouns not verbs. Ignoring these constraints leads to illegal label sequences. Another misconception is over-reliance on large models; for domain-specific entity types (e.g., medical terms, legal clauses), rule-based or dictionary methods may be more accurate and efficient.

Failure modes include: training noise from inconsistent annotations, low recall for rare entities, difficulty recognizing nested entities. For diagnosis, analyze misclassification patterns of specific entity types in confusion matrices, checking whether errors are boundary recognition mistakes (B/I label confusion) or type recognition mistakes (LOC/ORG confusion). For long entities, boundary precision (proportion of exact boundary matches) can be computed.

After mastering mechanisms for assigning discrete labels, we turn to more creative tasks: how to make models generate coherent, relevant, and diverse text? This requires deep understanding of the probabilistic modeling essence of text generation.

Engineering Practice: Building Reproducible NLP Task Pipelines

Text generation tasks require models to generate coherent text outputs based on inputs, covering applications like machine translation, summarization, and dialogue systems. Mathematically, generation models need to model the conditional probability distribution \(P(y|x)\), where \(y = (y_1, y_2, ..., y_M)\) is the output sequence. Autoregressive generation decomposes this probability via chain rule: \[P(y|x) = \prod_{t=1}^{M} P(y_t | y_{<t}, x)\] each timestep predicting the next token based on previously generated prefix and input. The objective function is negative log-likelihood: \[\mathcal{L}_{NLL} = -\sum_{t=1}^{M} \log P(y_t | y_{<t}, x)\]

Traditional statistical methods like n-gram language models rely on Markov assumptions, considering only limited historical context. Neural generation models use RNN, LSTM, or Transformer to encode input and decode output. Modern large language models guide generation through prompt engineering: designing prompt templates \(\text{prompt}(x)\) for models to complete subsequent text. For example, a summarization prompt could be "Please generate a summary for the following article: {article content}\nSummary:". The core of prompt engineering is finding expressions that elicit relevant knowledge from models while controlling generation style and format.

Evaluating generation quality is a core challenge. Automatic evaluation metric ROUGE (Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation) computes based on n-gram overlap: \[\text{ROUGE-N} = \frac{\sum_{S\in\{\text{reference summaries}\}} \sum_{\text{gram}_n\in S} \text{Count}_{\text{match}}(\text{gram}_n)}{\sum_{S\in\{\text{reference summaries}\}} \sum_{\text{gram}_n\in S} \text{Count}(\text{gram}_n)}\] where N is n-gram length, \(\text{Count}_{\text{match}}\) is the number of n-grams shared between generated and reference summaries. ROUGE-1 focuses on unigram overlap, ROUGE-2 on bigram overlap, ROUGE-L on longest common subsequence.

Engineering implementation must ensure reproducibility: fixing random seeds, recording dependency versions, saving intermediate results. Data pipelines should include cleaning (removing HTML tags, normalizing whitespace), tokenization (choosing word, character, or subword units per task), splitting (stratified to maintain class distribution). Model training should monitor train/validation loss curves to prevent overfitting. Deployment must consider generation speed (affected by decoding algorithms and sequence length) and memory usage (model parameter count).

A common misconception is that "high accuracy means the model is good." For generation tasks, high ROUGE scores may correspond to fluent but irrelevant text, or relevant but redundant text. Human evaluation should complement to check faithfulness (whether original meaning is distorted), coherence (whether logic is smooth), and informativeness (whether key information is included). Another misconception is neglecting the systematic nature of prompt engineering: prompts should be optimized via A/B testing, recording performance differences across templates.

Failure modes include: generating repetitive content (due to insufficient diversity in beam search), generating irrelevant content (due to attention mechanism failure), generating unsafe content (due to biases in training data). For diagnosis, analyze error types in generated samples, adjust decoding parameters (e.g., temperature, top-p), modify prompt templates, or add post-processing rules. For critical applications, establish regression test sets to monitor performance changes after model updates.

Now, let's translate this theoretical knowledge into concrete code, building a complete text classification system to experience the full pipeline from data to evaluation.

Reproducible Example: News Text Classification System

The following code builds an end-to-end news text classification system using scikit-learn's built-in 20newsgroups dataset (Source: Scikit-learn: Machine Learning in Python, 2011). We implement a complete pipeline of TF-IDF feature extraction + logistic regression, compute accuracy and F1-score, and visualize confusion matrix for error analysis.

# Code Block #1: End-to-End News Text Classification System
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.datasets import fetch_20newsgroups
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, f1_score, confusion_matrix
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

# Fix random seed for reproducibility
np.random.seed(42)

# 1. Load dataset and check basic information
data = fetch_20newsgroups(subset='all', remove=('headers', 'footers', 'quotes'))
print(f"Dataset shape: {len(data.data)} samples, {len(data.target_names)} categories")
print(f"First 3 categories: {data.target_names[:3]}")
print(f"Sample text (first 200 chars): {data.data[0][:200]}...")
print(f"Corresponding label: {data.target_names[data.target[0]]}")

# 2. Split train, validation, test sets (stratify to maintain class distribution)
X_temp, X_test, y_temp, y_test = train_test_split(
    data.data, data.target, test_size=0.2, random_state=42, stratify=data.target
)
X_train, X_val, y_train, y_val = train_test_split(
    X_temp, y_temp, test_size=0.25, random_state=42, stratify=y_temp  # 0.25 * 0.8 = 0.2
)
print(f"Train set: {len(X_train)} samples, Validation set: {len(X_val)} samples, Test set: {len(X_test)} samples")

# 3. Build TF-IDF + Logistic Regression pipeline
pipeline = Pipeline([
    ('tfidf', TfidfVectorizer(max_features=10000, stop_words='english')),
    ('clf', LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, random_state=42))
])

# Train model
pipeline.fit(X_train, y_train)

# 4. Evaluate model
val_pred = pipeline.predict(X_val)
val_accuracy = accuracy_score(y_val, val_pred)
val_f1 = f1_score(y_val, val_pred, average='macro')
print(f"Validation accuracy: {val_accuracy:.4f}")
print(f"Validation macro-average F1-score: {val_f1:.4f}")

# Final evaluation on test set
test_pred = pipeline.predict(X_test)
test_accuracy = accuracy_score(y_test, test_pred)
test_f1 = f1_score(y_test, test_pred, average='macro')
print(f"Test accuracy: {test_accuracy:.4f}")
print(f"Test macro-average F1-score: {test_f1:.4f}")

# 5. Confusion matrix visualization
cm = confusion_matrix(y_test, test_pred)
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 10))
sns.heatmap(cm, annot=True, fmt='d', cmap='Blues', 
            xticklabels=data.target_names, yticklabels=data.target_names)
plt.title('Confusion Matrix for 20 Newsgroups Classification')
plt.xlabel('Predicted Label')
plt.ylabel('True Label')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# 6. Error analysis: identify most confused category pairs
confusion_pairs = []
for i in range(len(data.target_names)):
    for j in range(len(data.target_names)):
        if i != j and cm[i, j] > 5:  # ignore minor misclassifications
            confusion_pairs.append((data.target_names[i], data.target_names[j], cm[i, j]))
confusion_pairs.sort(key=lambda x: x[2], reverse=True)
print("\nMost confused category pairs (misclassified samples >5):")
for true_label, pred_label, count in confusion_pairs[:5]:
    print(f"  {true_label} → {pred_label}: {count} samples")

# 7. Record key information
print("\nKey dependency versions:")
import sklearn
print(f"scikit-learn: {sklearn.__version__}")
print(f"numpy: {np.__version__}")
print(f"Random seed: 42")

Running this code outputs dataset size, number of categories, sample text, and computes test accuracy and macro-average F1-score. Confusion matrix visualization shows misclassification patterns across categories, with error analysis identifying most confused category pairs (e.g., "comp.sys.ibm.pc.hardware" vs "comp.sys.mac.hardware"). This implementation is fully self-contained, requiring no external data files, and reproducible in any environment with scikit-learn installed.

To replace with deep learning models, substitute the TF-IDF vectorizer with BERT feature extractor: use transformers library to load pre-trained BERT model, extract hidden states of [CLS] token as features, then feed into the same logistic regression classifier. Note deep models require GPU acceleration and have significantly higher inference latency than traditional methods.

Through this course, we systematically organized definitions, mechanisms, and engineering practices for four core NLP tasks. Classification learns discrete label mappings, sequence labeling models token-level dependencies, generation autoregressively predicts sequences, evaluation quantifies model performance. Each task has suitable mathematical tools, implementation points, and evaluation standards. Mastering this task map enables you to choose appropriate technical paths based on specific needs, whether building traditional machine learning pipelines or designing large language model prompts. Next, explore how Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) combines retrieval and generation tasks, or delve into design principles of LLM evaluation metrics.

title.zh: 视觉模型部署要点：预处理、批处理、延迟与显存
title.en: Key Points for Visual Model Deployment: Preprocessing, Batch Processing, Latency, and GPU Memory

summary.zh: 本课程深入探讨视觉模型部署中的核心工程挑战，系统讲解预处理、批处理、延迟与显存的平衡机制。课程首先分析预处理与批处理对性能瓶颈的影响，建立硬件利用率与显存占用的数学模型。其次，提供延迟、吞吐和显存的量化测量方法，引入Little定律与准确率公式作为评估基准。最后，探讨动态批处理策略与显存优化技术，通过约束优化问题形式化工程权衡。示例部分构建可复现的部署管线，使用CIFAR-10数据集和ResNet-18模型，量化不同批处理大小下的性能指标，并可视化延迟与显存的变化曲线。
summary.en: This course delves into the core engineering challenges of visual model deployment, systematically explaining the balancing mechanisms among preprocessing, batching, latency, and memory. It first analyzes the impact of preprocessing and batching on performance bottlenecks, establishing mathematical models for hardware utilization and memory footprint. Next, it provides quantitative measurement methods for latency, throughput, and memory, introducing Little's Law and the accuracy formula as evaluation benchmarks. Finally, it explores dynamic batching strategies and memory optimization techniques, formalizing engineering trade-offs through constrained optimization problems. The example section constructs a reproducible deployment pipeline using the CIFAR-10 dataset and ResNet-18 model, quantifying performance metrics under different batch sizes and visualizing latency and memory change curves.
